# Bastion

Bastion is a software factory that runs on your own machine. A request goes in,
agents work it through a pipeline of stages, and a reviewed change comes out.
Nothing merges itself. It's a native app (Tauri 2, Leptos, Rust) on the
[iii](https://iii.dev) engine, and it's early: the app shell, Doctor and the
stack controls work, and the factory itself starts in phase A3 of
[PLAN.md](PLAN.md).

```sh
cargo tauri dev
```

That opens the app. Go to **Engine**, press **Start**, and Bastion runs Doctor,
then brings up the stack in `worker-compose.yaml`. If the stack already runs,
the app attaches to it instead of starting a second one.

## What it is not

Not an editor: the only code you see in Bastion is the diff a job proposes. Not
a web app yet: the page runs in the native window and talks to its Bastion
servers over HTTP. It runs locally by default; a shared Bastion server can take
several people, each signing in with a token the server issued them. Not
Windows, because sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`.

## What you need

- Rust, from `rust-toolchain.toml` (rustup picks it up), and the
  `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target.
- `cargo install tauri-cli trunk`.
---PLAN
# Bastion plan

Bastion is a harness and a factory for agent work, on the iii engine. A
request goes in, a reviewed change comes out, and nothing merges itself. What
Bastion adds is governance you can measure: constraints and capabilities built
into the harness's hooks, a way to promote and demote each one, a
tamper-evident audit record, and A/B evals that show what a change to the
harness does. It is one app: a Tauri 2 window with a Leptos frontend and a Rust
core, against a local engine that the app starts. A remote engine on the
owner's own box comes later (§10). Written 2026-10-30, revised the same day.

It is general. The owner sets up their own accounts and settings so Bastion
uses the processes, products, tools and policies they already use: their forge,
their tracker, their CI, their model providers, their pipeline and their rules.

**The words** (used the same way everywhere in Bastion):

- **Charter:** a project's own rules, written by people and kept in the
  project: its `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, and the constraints and capabilities
  it declares. Each workspace has a charter, or runs without one on the owner's
  defaults.
- **Harness:** what runs one agent turn and applies the charter to it. Hooks
  check each call against the constraints and capabilities in force. Bastion is
  a harness.
- **Factory:** the pipeline of stages and checkpoints that turns a request into
  a landed change, with turns in the harness at its agent stages. Bastion is a
  factory.
- **Constraint:** a rule about what a turn must or must not do, on a ladder:
  told (in the brief), checked (a hook records breaches), enforced (a hook
  refuses the call).

An illustration of the Jobs page. The jobs that wait on you come first.

The problem

Agents write code fast. Trusting what they wrote is the slow part.

The report isn't the work

An agent can say it finished work that its commits don't hold. The gap shows up in the diff, if anyone reads it.

Rules in a prompt drift

A prompt can say "keep the tests," but nothing measures whether the agent listened. So there's no way to tell if a stricter rule helps or only costs more.

The agent holds your keys

An agent that can push and merge has your credentials in its run. And a run that has seen a credential can't be trusted again.

Sessions don't add up

Five agents in five terminals is five things to watch, and nothing says which one is waiting.

The solution

Treat each request as a job, and keep every decision that matters with you.

One board for every job

Each request becomes a job with its own worktree and sandbox VM. The Jobs page shows them all, with the ones waiting on you first.

You judge artifacts, not claims

Every stage leaves something you can check, such as a plan, a test result, or a diff. A comment on one goes to the agent as its next brief.

Rules you can measure

Every rule is a hook decision with a level: told, checked, or enforced. Run an eval to see what a stricter level does before you commit to it.

Keys stay out of the sandbox

Agents run in sandbox VMs that never see a credential. Pushes and pull requests happen on the host, and a tamper-evident log records every decision.

# Voice check

**`~/.claude/VOICE.md` is the standard and the only source of truth. Read it
first, every time. Do not review from memory of it, and do not restate its rules
here.** This file only covers how to run the check.

This is the authoritative stage of the VOICE.md section 15 chain, and the only
one that rewrites nothing. `humanizer` handles tone and `slopbeth` handles slop,
but both rewrite, so both can hand back what this skill already rejected. That
is why it runs first to set the constraints and again at the end as the gate.

It also catches what neither of them can: Ian's own formula, and drift between
pieces.

## Steps

1. Read `~/.claude/VOICE.md`.
2. Run the checker:
   ```bash
   python3 ~/.claude/skills/voice-check/voicecheck.py PATH \
     --corpus ~/tacoda/tacoda.github.io
   ```
   `PATH` takes a file or a directory. HTML is stripped to prose; code blocks,
   styles and scripts are excluded. `--corpus` enables recycled-phrase detection
   against the published body of work. Exits non-zero when there are findings.
3. Add `--show-flow 2` to print the paragraphs where sentences stop connecting.
   That is the fastest way to fix what reads as cold.
4. Run `humanizer` for tone, then `slopbeth` for slop, then this checker again
   as the gate. Both rewriters run under the findings from step 2 as hard
   constraints: neither may reintroduce a banned phrase, an em dash, or a tic
   already over budget, and neither may add a claim, number, or first-person
   experience the draft does not already contain. A finding that reappears at
   the gate gets fixed in the rewriter that put it back.
5. **Read the prose.** The script reports signals, not judgment. It cannot see a
   section that answers no reader question, an aphorism doing the work a
   mechanism should do, or a missing concession.
6. Report or fix, per what was asked, quoting the exact span for each finding.

## Reading the output

Findings marked `[advisory]` are the deliberate-structure cases in VOICE.md §5:
parallel rubric labels, non-goals lists, data triads. They usually mean leave it
alone. Everything else is a real finding.

Two metrics are easy to misread:

- `reader address` counts "you"/"your" **and** imperatives, so a page of
  instructions scores correctly without contorting into second person.
- `flow` is measured only inside paragraphs of three or more sentences. A
  reference page made of tables and captions is not scored on it.
- `over length` counts body prose only, so a page sitting near the 4,500-word cap
  is longer than that in wall-clock time once its code blocks and tables are
  read. VOICE.md §16 says what to cut and in what order.

## Rules

- **Preserve every fact.** Numbers, counts, dates, repo names, stated
  uncertainty, and non-goals survive any rewrite.
- **Never invent** first-person experience to hit the "I" floor. That floor is a
  request for a fact only Ian has. Ask him for it.
- **Do not trade one formula for another.** Replacing negation-definitions with
  clipped aphorisms is not a fix, and splitting a joined clause into two flat
  sentences to kill an em dash makes the prose worse, not better.
- **Over-editing strong prose is a failure.** Targets are ranges, not gates. A
  deliberate violation that serves the reader is fine; say why in the report.

I've rebranded the site, README.md, and PLAN.md. Nothing is committed or pushed yet, so you can read the wording first.

**Site** (`bastion-gh-pages/index.html`):
- **Title and heading:** "Agent workflows as graphs you can see and govern."
- **Header label:** "· control plane". It replaces "· software factory", and the header still fits on one row at 1001px.
- **Lede:** "Bastion is an agent orchestration control plane, built on iii. A workflow is a graph of steps: skills, prompts, commands, and Bastion's own stages. Give it a request, and agents work each step in a sandbox while you choose which steps wait for you, merge included. It's early, and the canvas for editing workflows is still in progress."
- **Meta description and the oversight section:** I changed these the same way. "A new factory waits" is now "A new workflow waits".
- **New line in the workflows section:** "If you know LangGraph, a step is a node and a link is an edge. The difference is that a link carries a result, not a condition, and the steps run on iii, in the job's sandbox VM."

**README.md:** the opening paragraph now uses the same positioning.

**PLAN.md:**
- The opening sentence now calls Bastion an agent orchestration control plane.
- I added decision **D37** for the new positioning. It keeps the name Bastion and keeps "charter", "harness", and "factory" as layer names, with the factory as the layer that runs a workflow. Code names like `factory.rs` and `/api/factory` don't change.

The voice check found nothing in the new text. Its 2 findings were already there before my change: the ladder section's choppy sentences, and no first person in the README. I didn't run the humanizer and slopbeth steps of the voice chain on these few sentences, since the check found nothing in them to fix.

The GitHub repo description on tacoda/bastion probably still says "software factory". I didn't change it.

Should I commit both repos and push the site?
commit both and push the site
